demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
The event happened because of the way I acted
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the trigger set is clinically incoherent. All three triggers are positively valenced interpersonal cues (affection, praise, positive emotion) with no trauma-specific or guilt-linked cue; as a trio they are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and with this trauma type, where reminders of responsibility, injury, driving/scene cues, or criticism are more plausible. While one such item could occur idiosyncratically, all three together are implausible.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I am permanently an outsider now' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile and trauma type. The other appraisals center on guilt and diminished capability, which fit accidental injury, but a stable outsider/alienation identity is not well supported by the selected triggers or memory items and is more characteristic of chronic interpersonal trauma or stigmatized victimization. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a coherent guilt-based formulation.

vignette: Sita is a 31-year-old South Asian woman who has been struggling with intense distress following a traumatic event. Married and working as a teacher in a local middle school, Sita's life took an unexpected turn when she accidentally caused serious injury to another person. The incident occurred during a field trip where she was responsible for overseeing the students' safety. Despite her best efforts, one of her students fell from a platform and sustained severe injuries. In the aftermath of the accident, Sita's world became a different place. She found herself haunted by the memory of that moment-each vivid snapshot replayed in her mind as if it were happening right then. The scent of the outdoors, the smell of sunscreen and grass, brought the event back with a stark immediacy. Every time she thought about the accident, she could almost feel the sun beating down on her skin and hear the panicked cries that followed. Sita's daily life became increasingly challenging as she grappled with triggers that seemed to be everywhere. Being praised for her work or receiving positive attention at school only exacerbated her distress. Positive emotions now felt overwhelming and confusing, often leaving her feeling disoriented and anxious. Discussions about accidents in general could send her into a spiral of fear and self-doubt. Since the incident, Sita has come to believe that she is no longer capable of doing the things that once defined her as an accomplished teacher. Her self-blame has grown to dominate her thoughts, constantly reminding her that the event happened because of her actions-or lack thereof. This sense of incapability seeped into her professional life; she began to avoid taking on new responsibilities and found herself struggling with even routine tasks. Sita's social interactions have also been deeply affected. She feels like an outsider among colleagues and friends, as though no one can truly understand what she has gone through. Her husband, while supportive, has noticed a growing distance in their relationship. Sita's avoidance behaviors extended to her personal life; she found herself canceling plans with friends and avoiding social gatherings where praise or positive emotions might come up. Over time, these changes began to have concrete consequences on her daily life. Students noticed that their once enthusiastic teacher seemed distant and preoccupied. Her colleagues observed a decline in her engagement during staff meetings and collaborative projects. Sita's performance evaluations reflected this change; she received less positive feedback than before, reinforcing her negative self-appraisals. The culmination of these struggles finally brought Sita to seek help. She realized that her ability to function was deteriorating, both at work and at home. What frightened her most was the fear of becoming permanently disconnected from those around her-both professionally and personally. She hoped that with therapy, she could regain a sense of normalcy and reconnect with the people in her life. As Sita begins this journey toward recovery, she is most afraid of reliving the trauma and feeling like an outsider forever. Yet, beneath her fears lies a deep hope for healing-a chance to reclaim her identity as a capable teacher and a valued member of her community.
